comment: Requirements are selected by the same declarative predicates as primitives. Each is written so that two independent implementers would build something a shared test suite accepts. Failure paths are mandatory: a requirement without a failure path is a demo script.

requirements.title: Runnable from a clean clone
requirements.statement: A new contributor can install dependencies, start the project and run its tests from a clean clone using only the documented commands, with no manual database seeding, no hidden local state and no undocumented environment variables.
requirements.definition: A clean clone of {project} runs with one documented command, and a missing setting is named rather than guessed.
requirements.failurePath: A missing environment variable produces a single actionable error naming the variable, not a stack trace deep in a startup path.
acceptance: Given a fresh clone and an empty environment file, when the documented setup command runs, then it either succeeds or lists every missing required variable by name.

requirements.title: The primary journey works end to end
requirements.statement: The single journey described in the product brief works from first step to last, through the real interface, persisting whatever it must persist, and produces the outcome the brief promises. It is exercised by one end-to-end test, not by unit tests of its parts.
requirements.definition: One {primary} goes from created to finished end to end through the documented interface, with no manual step in the middle and nothing reachable only by a developer.
requirements.failurePath: If any step of the journey fails, the user is left in a state they can retry from, with no partially written data and an explanation that names what failed.
acceptance: Given a new user and empty storage, when they complete the primary journey using only the documented interface, then the outcome named in the brief exists and is readable on a second visit.
Given the same journey, when a dependency it relies on is unavailable, then the user sees an actionable message and no partial record is created.

requirements.title: Explicit non-goals
requirements.statement: The product brief lists at least three things this version deliberately does not do, and the codebase contains no partially built version of them.
requirements.definition: The three things {project} will not do in v1 are written down, reviewed before the first sprint, and cited the first time someone asks for a fourth thing.
requirements.failurePath: Out-of-scope work arrives as a failing review comment referencing a non-goal, rather than as silent extra code.
acceptance: Given the brief, when a reviewer reads the change, then every capability in the diff maps to an in-scope requirement or is rejected.

requirements.title: Durable state with forward-only migrations
requirements.statement: Persistent state is defined by a schema kept in version control. Every schema change ships as a forward-only migration that can run on a non-empty database without data loss.
requirements.definition: What {project} knows about {aPrimary} survives a restart in {db}, and every schema change is a forward-only migration with a restore step that has been run once.
requirements.failurePath: A migration that fails halfway leaves the database in a known state, and the documented restore step returns it to the pre-migration snapshot.
acceptance: Given a database at the previous schema version with representative rows, when the migration runs, then all rows remain readable and no column required by the new code is null.
Given the same database, when the migration is re-run, then it is a no-op rather than an error.

requirements.title: Data lifecycle: retention, export and deletion
requirements.statement: Every personal data field has a documented purpose, retention period and deletion path. A single operation removes all data belonging to one subject, including derived rows and cached copies.
requirements.definition: A {secondary}'s {primary} data has a stated retention period, an export, and a deletion path that removes every copy including the ones in logs and fixtures.
requirements.failurePath: A deletion request for an unknown subject returns success without inventing records, and leaves no orphan rows.
acceptance: Given a subject with records in every table, when deletion runs, then a query for that subject across all tables returns zero rows.
Given a deletion request, when the audit log is inspected, then the request is recorded without storing the deleted personal data.

requirements.title: Authentication with explicit session lifecycle
requirements.statement: Users authenticate through a named mechanism. Sessions expire, can be revoked, and never rely on client-held claims that the server cannot verify.
requirements.definition: A {secondary} signs in and signs out, and a revoked session stops working on the server immediately rather than at the next token expiry.
requirements.failurePath: An expired or revoked session receives an unauthenticated response and performs no state change.
acceptance: Given valid credentials, when the user signs in, then a session is issued and the identifier is not placed in a URL.
Given a revoked session, when any protected endpoint is called, then the response is 401 and no data is written.
Given a sign-out-everywhere request, when any previously issued session is used, then all are rejected except the current one.

requirements.title: Server-side authorization with deny-by-default
requirements.statement: Every state-changing operation and every read of another subject's data checks permission on the server, keyed to a named role or policy, with deny as the default.
requirements.definition: Reading or changing another {secondary}'s {primary} is refused by the server; the interface is allowed to hide the control but never to be the control.
requirements.failurePath: A forbidden request returns 403 or 404 as documented, writes nothing, and emits an authorization-denied log line without leaking the resource's contents.
acceptance: Given a user without the required role, when the operation is attempted directly against the API, then it is refused even if the UI hides the control.
Given a resource owned by another subject, when it is requested by identifier, then the response does not reveal existence.

requirements.title: Tenant isolation
requirements.statement: Every unit of work belongs to exactly one tenant. The tenant key is applied by the layer that owns data access, never by individual call sites, and an inbound tenant identifier is never trusted.
requirements.definition: Two {secondaryPlural} in different tenants cannot see or affect each other's {primary} data through any query, handler or export path.
requirements.failurePath: A query constructed without a tenant filter fails closed (returns no rows or raises), rather than returning all tenants.
acceptance: Given two tenants with records, when tenant A lists records, then no tenant B identifier appears.
Given a forged tenant identifier, when it is processed, then it is rejected before any record is returned or changed.

requirements.title: Accessible primary journey
requirements.statement: The primary journey is completable with a keyboard only and with a screen reader, with visible focus, labelled controls and no colour-only status encoding.
requirements.definition: The main {primary} journey completes with a keyboard and a screen reader, error states included, and focus lands somewhere sensible after every navigation.
requirements.failurePath: Validation errors are announced and focus moves to the first invalid field, rather than the form silently failing.
acceptance: Given the primary journey, when it is driven by keyboard only, then every control is reachable and the outcome is completed.
Given a form submission with an invalid field, when it fails, then an error message is programmatically associated with that field and announced.

requirements.title: Every screen has loading, empty, error and success states
requirements.statement: Each data-driven screen defines four states before it is considered done, and the empty state tells the user the next action.
requirements.definition: Every {primary} screen has loading, empty, error and success states, and the error state carries the next action rather than an apology.
requirements.failurePath: A failed request shows a retry affordance and preserves the user's input rather than discarding the form.
acceptance: Given a slow response, when the screen loads, then a loading state appears within 200ms and does not shift layout.
Given zero records, when the screen loads, then an empty state with a single next action is shown.
Given a server error, when the request fails, then an error state with a working retry is shown.

requirements.title: One design token source
requirements.statement: Colour, spacing, typography and radius come from a single token source. No component hard-codes a hex colour, pixel spacing value or font family.
requirements.definition: Colour, spacing and type come from one token source, so restyling the {primary} views is a change to one file and not to every component.
requirements.failurePath: A component using a raw value fails the design-token fitness check in CI.
acceptance: Given the component directory, when the token check runs, then no raw colour or spacing literal is reported.

requirements.title: Errors are classified before they are rendered
requirements.statement: Errors are classified as user-correctable, retryable or unexpected, and each class has one documented presentation and logging rule.
requirements.definition: A {primary} failure is classified before it is rendered, so the message tells the {secondary} what to do next and never leaks an identifier they cannot act on.
requirements.failurePath: Unexpected errors never render internal messages, stack traces or identifiers to the user, and are logged with a correlation ID that is shown as a short support code.
acceptance: Given a forced internal failure, when it is displayed, then the user sees a generic message plus a support code and the server log contains the matching correlation ID.

requirements.title: Versioned machine-readable interface contract
requirements.statement: Every exposed or consumed interface is described in a machine-readable contract kept in the repository, and breaking changes are detected before merge.
requirements.definition: The {primary} interface has a versioned, machine-readable contract kept in the repository, and a breaking change fails before merge rather than after a consumer notices.
requirements.failurePath: An incompatible change fails the contract check and names the field and the consumer affected.
acceptance: Given the contract and the implementation, when the contract check runs, then they agree on paths, methods, status codes and error shape.
Given a removed response field, when the check runs, then it fails as a breaking change.

requirements.title: One error envelope and one identifier scheme
requirements.statement: All errors share one envelope containing a stable machine code, a human message, a correlation ID and optional field details. Identifiers are opaque and are never sequential integers in public interfaces.
requirements.definition: Every failure on the {primary} interface returns one envelope shape, with an opaque identifier a support conversation can quote.
requirements.failurePath: An unknown route and a failed validation return the same envelope shape with distinguishable machine codes.
acceptance: Given an invalid payload, when the response is inspected, then its shape matches the documented envelope and the machine code is stable across releases.

requirements.title: Idempotent handling of retried work
requirements.statement: Every inbound webhook and every outbound retry is idempotent: replaying the same event produces the same end state and no duplicate side effect.
requirements.definition: A retried {primary} request produces the same outcome as the first one: no second record, no second side effect, no second notification.
requirements.failurePath: A duplicate event is acknowledged without reprocessing, and a retry storm does not create duplicate records or double-charge.
acceptance: Given the same event delivered twice, when both are processed, then exactly one record exists and one side effect occurred.
Given a client error from the upstream service (400/401/403), when the call fails, then it is not retried.
Given a 5xx or timeout, when the call fails, then it is retried with exponential backoff and jitter up to a documented cap.

requirements.title: Money movement is correct under retries and partial failure
requirements.statement: Amounts are stored in integer minor units with an explicit currency. Every charge, refund and transfer is idempotent, recorded in an append-only ledger, and reconciled against the provider.
requirements.definition: Money attached to {aPrimary} stays correct through retries, partial failure and reversal, because every correction is a new entry rather than an edit.
requirements.failurePath: A webhook arriving before the checkout response, or twice, results in exactly one entitlement and one ledger entry.
acceptance: Given a payment intent confirmed twice with the same idempotency key, when both requests are handled, then one charge exists.
Given a provider timeout after a successful capture, when reconciliation runs, then the local ledger converges to the provider's state without creating a second charge.
Given any ledger entry, when the totals are recomputed, then sums reconcile to zero across debits and credits for settled transactions.

requirements.title: Model calls are bounded, observable and evaluated
requirements.statement: Every model call has a declared input contract, an output validator, a timeout, a per-user rate limit and a cost ceiling. A versioned evaluation set exists for the prompts that matter.
requirements.definition: Model calls that touch {primary} content have a timeout, a validated response, a cost ceiling, and a recorded fixture the evaluation runs against.
requirements.failurePath: A malformed model response is rejected and the user sees a retryable message; it is never rendered as trusted markup.
acceptance: Given a model returning text outside the expected schema, when the response is processed, then it is rejected, logged and not shown to the user verbatim.
Given a session exceeding its token budget, when another call is attempted, then it is refused with a user-visible explanation.
Given the evaluation set, when a prompt changes, then the run reports pass rate before and after.

requirements.title: Observable behaviour under failure
requirements.statement: Every inbound request has a correlation ID propagated through logs and outbound calls. Errors, latency and queue depth are recorded in a form that can be alerted on.
requirements.definition: A failed {primary} operation is visible in a log with a correlation id the support team can search, without attaching a debugger to production.
requirements.failurePath: A failing dependency produces log lines carrying the correlation ID and an alertable error-rate increase, not a silent retry loop.
acceptance: Given a failing dependency, when a request is traced, then its log lines share one correlation ID and include the dependency name and outcome.

requirements.title: Abuse limits on public entry points
requirements.statement: Public write and authentication endpoints are rate limited per identity and per IP, with a documented response that includes a retry hint.
requirements.definition: Public entry points that create or change {primary} data are limited per identity and per address, and say how long to wait when they refuse.
requirements.failurePath: Exceeding the limit returns 429 with a retry hint and performs no work; the limiter fails closed for authentication endpoints.
acceptance: Given N+1 requests within the window, when the last is made, then it is refused with 429 and no state change occurred.

requirements.title: Append-only audit trail for privileged actions
requirements.statement: Privileged and destructive actions append an immutable record of actor, action, target, time and outcome. Records are never updated or deleted by application code.
requirements.definition: Privileged changes to {aPrimary} are append-only and attributable to the {secondary} who made them, including the ones made by a support tool.
requirements.failurePath: A failed privileged action is still recorded, with its failure reason and without sensitive payloads.
acceptance: Given a privileged action, when it completes or fails, then exactly one audit record exists and the application user has no update or delete grant on that table.

requirements.title: Reprocessable pipeline stages
requirements.statement: Each stage is deterministic given its inputs, records its watermark, and can be replayed for a time window without duplicating output.
requirements.definition: Re-running a window of {primary} data replaces its output instead of duplicating it, so a failed run is safe to retry rather than a reason to clean up by hand.
requirements.failurePath: Replaying a window produces identical output and leaves row counts unchanged.
acceptance: Given a completed run, when the same window is replayed, then the output partition is byte-identical and row counts are unchanged.

requirements.title: Stable public surface with semantic versioning
requirements.statement: The public export surface is enumerated and tested, so an accidental breaking change fails CI. Versions follow semantic versioning.
requirements.definition: The public surface, described in terms of {aPrimary}, is versioned; removing or changing anything a consumer can call requires a major version and a migration note.
requirements.failurePath: Removing or changing a public export fails the surface test and requires a major version bump.
acceptance: Given the recorded export surface, when the package is rebuilt, then the surface matches or the build fails.

requirements.title: Predictable command-line behaviour
requirements.statement: Commands follow a documented grammar, write data to stdout and diagnostics to stderr, support --help and --version, and exit non-zero on failure.
requirements.definition: Every command that touches {aPrimary} documents its flags and exit codes, rejects unknown input, and supports a dry run that changes nothing.
requirements.failurePath: An invalid flag prints usage to stderr and exits 2; a partial failure exits non-zero and leaves no half-written output file.
acceptance: Given an invalid flag, when the command runs, then usage goes to stderr, stdout is empty and the exit code is non-zero.

requirements.title: Spec drift is detected mechanically
requirements.statement: Requirements marked automated carry an @req anchor in the test that proves them. CI fails when an anchored requirement has no test, when a test cites an unknown requirement, or when a primitive referenced by the spec disappears.
requirements.definition: A requirement about {aPrimary} that loses its test anchor fails the build rather than passing quietly.
requirements.failurePath: Deleting a test that proves an automated requirement fails CI with the requirement identifier and the missing anchor.
acceptance: Given a requirement anchored to a deleted test, when CI runs, then it fails and names the requirement.
Given an @req anchor for an identifier absent from the spec, when CI runs, then it fails as unknown.

requirements.title: The product's own rules are named and pinned
requirements.statement: Every invariant listed in the domain model names a rule that makes this product itself, and each has at least one automated test whose failure mode is that rule being violated. An invariant with no test is a comment; a test that would pass with the rule inverted is not a test.
requirements.definition: The rules that make {aPrimary} valid are written down, and each one has a test that fails when the rule is broken rather than a comment saying it matters.
requirements.failurePath: If a core rule is inverted by a refactor, a test fails and names the rule, rather than the change being discovered by a user or a reviewer.
acceptance: Given the invariants listed in the domain model, when the suite runs, then each invariant is covered by a test that fails if its rule is inverted.
Given an invariant added to the domain model, when it has no test, then the review checklist rejects the change.

requirements.title: Uploads are validated, contained and stripped
requirements.statement: Every uploaded file is checked against an allowlist of types and a size limit before it is stored, stored under a generated name outside any directory the web server executes, and served only through an authorised or signed URL. Metadata that the product does not need, such as location, is removed on ingest.
requirements.definition: A file attached to {aPrimary} is type-checked by content, size-capped, stripped of metadata, and stored where the web server cannot execute it.
requirements.failurePath: An uploaded HTML file served from the asset host becomes stored XSS; a photo carrying GPS coordinates leaks the user's home address; an unbounded upload fills the disk and takes the service down.
acceptance: Given a file whose type or size is not allowed, when it is uploaded, then it is rejected with a named reason and nothing is written to storage.
Given an allowed image with location metadata, when it is stored, then the stored object contains no location metadata and is reachable only through an authorised URL.

requirements.title: Offline writes are durable and replay is safe
requirements.statement: A write made without a network is persisted locally before the interface reports success, survives the application being killed, and is replayed on reconnect without duplicating the effect. Conflicting writes follow one documented rule, and the interface shows what is still pending rather than implying it is saved.
requirements.definition: {aPrimary} changed while offline replays exactly once after reconnect, even if the app is killed between the write and the sync.
requirements.failurePath: A user ticks a habit on a train, closes the app, and the tick is gone; or it is replayed three times and the streak counts three.
acceptance: Given no network, when a write is made and the process is killed before reconnecting, then the write is present after restart and is eventually applied exactly once.
Given the same record edited on two devices while offline, when both reconnect, then the documented conflict rule decides the result and the loser is reported, not silently dropped.
